findings.title: requirements.txt omits cvxpy, matplotlib, seaborn — empirical experiments can't be installed
findings.quote:
import numpy as np
import cvxpy as cp
from tqdm import tqdm
import time
from multiprocessing import Pool
findings.claim: The entire optimization core (twosf_solver.py, fig1/fig2a/fig2b.py) imports cvxpy and matplotlib, and the evaluation notebook imports seaborn + matplotlib, but requirements.txt lists none of cvxpy, matplotlib, or seaborn.
findings.concern: A fresh `pip install -r requirements.txt` cannot run any of the fairness-tradeoff experiments (no cvxpy/matplotlib) or the Table-1 notebook (no seaborn), so the empirical results are not reproducible from the pinned environment.
findings.resolution: Add cvxpy, matplotlib, and seaborn (with pinned versions) to requirements.txt; ideally list the SCS solver too.
findings.reason: Lines 1-5 of twosf_solver.py match the quote exactly (imports cvxpy); repo-wide check confirms cvxpy and matplotlib.pyplot are imported (fig1/fig2a/fig2b.py, twosf_solver.py) and seaborn is imported in post_processing_evaluation.ipynb, yet requirements.txt (43 pinned packages) contains none of cvxpy, matplotlib, or seaborn.

findings.title: No code generates the SPECTER / Sentence-Transformer embeddings used in Table 1
findings.quote:
with open('./Data/train_matrix_transformer.pickle', 'rb') as f:
    tfidf_matrix_train_data = pickle.load(f)

with open('./Data/test_matrix_transformer.pickle', 'rb') as r:
    tfidf_matrix_test_data = pickle.load(r)
findings.claim: The Sentence-Transformer recommender only *loads* pre-computed embedding pickles; a repo-wide scan finds no `SentenceTransformer`, `SPECTER`, `.encode(`, or `allenai` anywhere in the .py or .ipynb files.
findings.concern: The paper (App. B.2) states embeddings are generated with 'the AllenAI SPECTER model', and two of Table 1's four rows are the Sentence-Transformer models; the step that produces those embeddings is absent, so those rows and the SPECTER-based analyses cannot be reproduced.
findings.resolution: Add the script that encodes titles/abstracts with SPECTER into `train_matrix_transformer.pickle` / `test_matrix_transformer.pickle` (model name, pooling, truncation), or ship the pickles.
findings.paper_ref: Appendix B.2 'Sentence Transformers ... AllenAI SPECTER model'; Table 1 rows 3–4
findings.reason: Lines 20-24 of sentence_transformer_authors.py match the quote exactly (only pickle.load of pre-made embedding matrices); a repo-wide grep for SentenceTransformer|SPECTER|.encode(|allenai across all .py/.ipynb returns zero hits, confirming no embedding-generation code exists.

findings.title: Headline '>47% of papers <0.0001% recommendation probability' has no computing code
findings.quote: we find that on average more than 47% of papers have less than a 0.0001% probability of being recommended to any user, even when the number of users and items are the same
findings.claim: This motivating empirical statistic requires computing a recommendation probability / exposure distribution over items; a repo-wide scan finds no code computing recommendation probabilities, argmax recommendations, or exposure (no `argmax`, `exposure`, `0.0001`, or probability-distribution computation in any .py/.ipynb).
findings.concern: A quantitative empirical claim placed in the Introduction is not backed by any script in the repository, so it cannot be verified or reproduced.
findings.resolution: Point to (or add) the script that computes per-item recommendation probability under the basic recommender and the 47% / 0.0001% threshold, including the 'equal number of users and items' setting.
findings.reason: The exact sentence '...more than 47% of papers have less than a 0.0001% probability of being recommended to any user, even when the number of users and items are the same' is present verbatim in the Introduction of paper_text.txt; a repo-wide scan for argmax/exposure/0.0001/1e-6/1e-4/prob_recommend across all .py/.ipynb returns zero hits (the only '47' hits are spurious digit matches, e.g. notebook execution counts), confirming no code computes this statistic.

findings.title: Appendix robustness figures (Nash, max-sum-k-min, asymmetric utility) have no implementing code
findings.claim: twosf_solver.py implements only the symmetric max-min (egalitarian) objective over a single utility matrix U; there is no Nash-welfare objective (sum log U), no sum-of-k-min objective, and no separate wI/wU asymmetric-utility path.
findings.concern: Appendix A Figures 2 (Nash welfare), 3 (max-sum-k-min, k=3), and 4–5 (asymmetric/exposure utility interpolation) are described as re-running the main experiment with these alternative formulations, but no code for those formulations exists, so the robustness checks are not reproducible.
findings.resolution: Provide the solver variants (Nash-welfare, k-min, asymmetric wI/wU) used to produce Appendix Figures 2–5, or state that these were computed by code not released.
findings.reason: Line 39 of twosf_solver.py matches the quote exactly; reading the full solver file (all cp.Problem/cp.Maximize calls) and grepping experiments/*.py for nash|log(|k_min|kmin|asymmetric|wI|wU shows only two max-min objective variants (user-given-item, item-given-user) exist — no Nash-welfare, k-min, or asymmetric-utility formulation anywhere in the codebase.

findings.title: tfidf_authors.py overwrites every recommendation's similarity_score with the last author's scores
findings.claim: Inside the per-author loop, `all_recommendations['similarity_score']` is recomputed for ALL accumulated rows by matching each row's paper title against the CURRENT author's `scores_per_paper`; after the final iteration every row holds the last-processed author's similarity for that title, not the author it was recommended to.
findings.concern: The exported TF-IDF `similarity_score` column is wrong for every author except the last, so any downstream use of this file (e.g. the Max-score-TF-IDF Table-1 citation regression, the paper's main-text model) would be computed on corrupted scores.
findings.resolution: Set `similarity_score` inside `recommend_papers` per author (as `sentence_transformer_authors.py:58` already does), not in a global overwrite; confirm which CSV fed Table 1 and whether it came from this buggy path.
findings.reason: Lines 123-130 of tfidf_authors.py match the quote exactly; this block sits inside the `for author in authors_list:` loop in recommend_for_authors, and scores_per_paper (rebuilt fresh per author from ALL test-set titles, not just recommended ones) is used to overwrite similarity_score for the FULL accumulated all_recommendations frame on every iteration. A faithful reproduction of this exact loop logic (2 authors, 2 shared titles) run in _verifier_code/aa_check_tfidf_score_overwrite.py confirms every row ends up holding the last author's (AuthorB's) score, not its own author's score (2 of 4 rows wrong, matching the described mechanism exactly).

findings.title: get_paper_details.py reads /Data/test_data.csv (root path) and never writes its output
findings.claim: README Step 3 tells users to run `get_paper_details.py`, but it opens the absolute path `/Data/test_data.csv` (leading slash → filesystem root) rather than `./Data/test_data.csv`, and the computed `data_s2` is never saved to disk.
findings.concern: The script crashes with FileNotFoundError on any normal checkout, and even if fixed produces no output file for the next pipeline stage, breaking the documented reproduction workflow.
findings.resolution: Change the path to `./Data/test_data.csv` and add the missing `data_s2.to_csv(...)` for the s2-id/corpusId table that later scripts consume.
findings.reason: Line 68 of get_paper_details.py matches the quote exactly (pd.read_csv("/Data/test_data.csv") with leading slash = filesystem root); the file is only 72 lines total and ends right after the dropna/drop_duplicates calls on data_s2 with no to_csv/to_pickle call anywhere, confirming the output is never persisted. README.md line 50 confirms `python3 get_paper_details.py` is the documented Step 3.

findings.title: Homogeneous tradeoff curves use every author in a cluster, not '500 random authors'
findings.quote:
m,n = W_restricted.shape
H = sample_utility(m, n, m,sample_n,W_restricted)
findings.claim: For the homogeneous curves, `sample_utility(m, n, m, sample_n, W_restricted)` sets sample_m = m = the full cluster size, so it uses ALL authors in the chosen k-means cluster; the diverse/random curves (`get_curves`) instead sample `sample_m` (=500) authors.
findings.concern: The paper (§6.1) states each homogeneous curve is formed from '200 random papers and 500 random authors from one random cluster', but the code uses every author in the cluster (~2000 with 20,512 users / 10 clusters); because the plotted quantity is a min over users, the homogeneous curve is a min over ~4x more users than the diverse curve, a population-size confound in the very comparison used to illustrate Theorem 3 (normalization by each population's own optimum only partly mitigates this).
findings.resolution: Confirm whether homogeneous curves used all cluster authors or a 500-author subsample; if the former, match author counts across the two curves (or state that results are insensitive to it).
findings.paper_ref: §6.1 'sampled 200 random papers and 500 random authors from one random cluster'
findings.reason: Lines 31-32 of experiments/fig2a.py match the quote exactly. sample_utility(m, n, sample_m, sample_n, W) does rng.choice(m, size=sample_m, replace=False); called as sample_utility(m, n, m, sample_n, W_restricted) with sample_m=m (the full cluster size from W_restricted.shape), so rng.choice(m, size=m, ...) samples every author in the cluster. The diverse-curve path (get_curves) instead passes a distinct sample_m argument from CLI. The paper's §6.1 text (verified in paper_text.txt) states '200 random papers and 500 random authors from one random cluster' for the homogeneous curves — the code contradicts this exactly as claimed.

findings.title: Table 1/3 'Adjusted R2' is actually McFadden pseudo-R2 from statsmodels Logit
findings.claim: The Table 1 and Table 3 goodness-of-fit column is labeled 'Adjusted R2', but the values are produced by `smf.logit(...).fit()` (post_processing_evaluation.ipynb cell 26), whose summary reports McFadden 'Pseudo R-squ.'; logistic regression has no OLS-style adjusted R2.
findings.concern: Readers may interpret 0.089–0.135 as an OLS adjusted R2 (variance explained) when it is a McFadden pseudo-R2 with a different scale and meaning.
findings.resolution: Relabel the column 'McFadden pseudo-R2' (or report it as such).
findings.reason: paper_text.txt confirms the 'Adjusted R2' column header appears in the Table 1/Table 3 regression tables (5 occurrences found, e.g. 'Max score, TF-IDF ... 0.08915'). post_processing_evaluation.ipynb cell 26 confirms the fitted model is smf.logit(...).fit() with results.summary() printed — statsmodels Logit has no OLS-style adjusted R2 and reports McFadden 'Pseudo R-squ.' in its summary, matching the claim exactly.

findings.title: Citation validation does not exclude the user's own 2020 papers (self-citation inflation)
findings.quote:
# Get the indices of the top 10 recommendations (excluding author's own papers)
# top_paper_indices = [i[0] for i in avg_sim_scores[:10]]
all_paper_indices = [i[0] for i in avg_sim_scores]
findings.claim: The candidate/recommendation pool is the entire test set with no exclusion of papers the user co-authored — the 'excluding author's own papers' line is commented out — so a user's own 2020 papers (textually most similar to their pre-2020 papers, and typically self-cited) remain in the pool and in the Table-1 'user cites paper' regression.
findings.concern: The notebook shows 1238 recommendations flagged `Also_Authored_by_input_author` with mean similarity 0.723 vs 0.612 overall (cell 18); these self-authored/self-cited pairs are not excluded from the citation-prediction regression, inflating the reported similarity→citation coefficient and pseudo-R2 that justify choosing the max-TF-IDF model.
findings.resolution: Re-run Table 1 with self-authored papers (Also_Authored_by_input_author == 1) removed and report whether the coefficients/pseudo-R2 survive.
findings.reason: Lines 83-85 of tfidf_authors.py match the quote exactly: the 'excluding author's own papers' top-10 line is commented out and all_paper_indices (the full candidate set) is used instead. post_processing_evaluation.ipynb cell 18 (dftodo.groupby('Also_Authored_by_input_author')[simcols].mean()) shows mean similarity_score 0.612734 for non-self-authored vs 0.723005 for self-authored, matching the cited '0.723 vs 0.612' numbers exactly. The specific '1238' row count was not independently located in the cited cell but the core mechanism and numeric evidence both check out.

findings.title: No RNG seeds anywhere — sampled curves and 1000-author selection are nondeterministic
findings.quote:
def sample_utility(m, n, sample_m,sample_n,W):
    rng = np.random.default_rng()
findings.claim: Every stochastic step uses an unseeded generator: `np.random.default_rng()` in experiment_utils/fig2a/fig2b, and `random.sample(...)` for the 1000-author selection in tfidf/sentence_transformer scripts; a repo-wide scan finds no `seed`/`random_state`/`default_rng(<int>)` anywhere.
findings.concern: The subsampled tradeoff curves, k-means clustering, misestimation subset, and the 1000-author validation sample cannot be reproduced exactly; run-to-run variation is bounded only by the reported std-error bars but the specific figures/tables are not regenerable.
findings.resolution: Seed numpy, python `random`, and sklearn (`random_state`) and document the seeds used for the reported figures/tables.
findings.reason: Lines 44-45 of experiments/experiment_utils.py match the quote exactly (np.random.default_rng() with no seed). A repo-wide grep for seed|random_state|default_rng(<int> across the entire repo returns zero hits, and random.sample(...) (also unseeded) is confirmed at tfidf_authors.py:142 and sentence_transformer_authors.py:89, matching the claim exactly.
